title: Media and opinion — speaking on the record
title_target: Di satu sisi…, di sisi lain…
goal: Give a balanced answer in a press interview and follow the argument of an Indonesian opinion piece. You will learn the connectors that hold a written argument together — and the spoken reactions people use when they read one.
bekal: weigh two sides with *di satu sisi … di sisi lain* and *namun demikian*
concede a point before pushing back: *tidak dapat dimungkiri bahwa…*, *harus diakui…*
draw a conclusion with *dengan demikian* and *oleh sebab itu*, and contrast with *tidak … melainkan*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Wawancara dengan Mbak Dewi
dialogs.intro: Early April. The budget with the university is settled (Unit 5), and the press has noticed. Mbak Dewi, education reporter for a national daily, interviews Sarah in the Program Jembatan office in Kuningan.

lines.speaker: Dewi:
lines.text: Terima kasih sudah bersedia diwawancarai, Bu Sarah. Boleh saya rekam?
lines.id: Thank you for agreeing to be interviewed. May I record this?
lines.literal: thank you already willing be-interviewed, Mrs Sarah. may I record?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Silakan, Mbak Dewi. Tapi panggil Sarah saja.
lines.id: Go ahead, Dewi. But just call me Sarah.
lines.literal: please, Miss Dewi. but call Sarah just.

lines.speaker: Dewi:
lines.text: Baik. Program Jembatan sering dikritik sebagai program elite. Bagaimana tanggapan Anda?
lines.id: All right. Program Jembatan is often criticised as an elite programme. What is your response?
lines.literal: good. programme Jembatan often is-criticised as programme elite. how response you?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Tidak dapat dimungkiri bahwa sebagian besar peserta tahun ini berasal dari kota besar.
lines.id: There's no denying that most of this year's participants come from big cities.
lines.literal: not can be-denied that part big participant year this originate from city big.

lines.speaker: Dewi:
lines.text: Jadi kritik itu benar?
lines.id: So the criticism is justified?
lines.literal: so criticism that true?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Sebagian benar. Di satu sisi, sekolah di kota memang lebih siap. Di sisi lain, justru sekolah di daerah yang paling membutuhkan program ini.
lines.id: Partly. On the one hand, city schools are better prepared. On the other, it's precisely the regional schools that need this programme most.
lines.literal: part true. at one side, school at city indeed more ready. at side other, precisely school at region that most need programme this.

lines.speaker: Dewi:
lines.text: Lalu apa langkah konkretnya?
lines.id: So what are the concrete steps?
lines.literal: then what step concrete-its?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Mulai tahun depan, empat puluh persen kuota kami sediakan bagi sekolah di luar Jawa.
lines.id: From next year we are reserving forty per cent of places for schools outside Java.
lines.literal: start year front, four ten percent quota we provide for school at outside Java.

lines.speaker: Dewi:
lines.text: Empat puluh persen. Dengan anggaran yang sama?
lines.id: Forty per cent. On the same budget?
lines.literal: four ten percent. with budget that same?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Anggarannya naik sedikit, berkat kesepakatan dengan pihak universitas bulan lalu.
lines.id: The budget has gone up slightly, thanks to last month's agreement with the university.
lines.literal: budget-the rise a-little, thanks-to agreement with side university month past.

lines.speaker: Dewi:
lines.text: Ada yang berpendapat bahwa pertukaran pelajar hanya menguntungkan pihak Australia.
lines.id: Some argue that student exchanges only benefit the Australian side.
lines.literal: exist who have-opinion that exchange student only benefit side Australia.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Saya kurang sependapat. Guru-guru kita pulang membawa metode baru, dan murid Australia pulang membawa bahasa Indonesia.
lines.id: I don't quite agree. Our teachers come home with new methods, and Australian students go home with Indonesian.
lines.literal: I less same-opinion. teacher-teacher our go-home carrying method new, and pupil Australia go-home carrying language Indonesia.

lines.speaker: Dewi:
lines.text: Kalimat itu bagus sekali. Boleh saya kutip?
lines.id: That's a very good line. May I quote it?
lines.literal: sentence that good very. may I quote?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Boleh, asal konteksnya tidak dipotong.
lines.id: Yes, as long as the context isn't cut.
lines.literal: may, provided context-its not is-cut.

notes: **Tidak dapat dimungkiri — "it cannot be denied".** This is the standard way to concede a point in formal Indonesian before you add your *but*. ⚠️ The baku root is *mungkir*, so the passive is *dimungkiri*; *dipungkiri* is everywhere, including in newspapers, but KBBI lists *pungkir* only as the non-standard form. Say either; write *dimungkiri*.

**Bersedia diwawancarai.** *Bersedia* (willing, prepared to) happily takes a passive after it: *bersedia diwawancarai*, *bersedia dihubungi* (willing to be contacted). Reporters ask *Boleh saya rekam?* as a courtesy; if you want something kept out of print, the phrase is *ini tidak untuk dikutip*, or simply the English *off the record*.

**Anda in an interview.** Face to face Dewi says *Bu Sarah*, but the question itself uses *Anda*. That is the press habit: *Anda* is neutral, printable and addresses the reader as much as the interviewee. In ordinary conversation the same *Anda* can sound cool, which is why Indonesians default to titles and names.

**Justru sekolah di daerah yang…** *Justru* (B1 Unit 9) flips an expectation: "it is *precisely* the regional schools that…". Combined with *yang*, it puts the spotlight on one noun. *Daerah* here means "the regions" — everywhere that is not a major city, and a politically loaded word in Jakarta.

**Saya kurang sependapat.** *Sependapat* is *se-* (one, same) + *pendapat* (opinion): "of the same opinion". *Kurang* (literally "less") turns a flat *tidak* into a polite "not quite". *Saya kurang setuju* and *saya kurang sependapat* are what a professional says when they mean "no".

**Asal konteksnya tidak dipotong.** *Asal* (short for *asalkan*) means "as long as, provided that". Every Indonesian public figure also knows the verb *dipelintir* — "twisted" — for a quote taken out of context. You will meet it in the second dialogue.

grammars.title: Weighing two sides
body: Formal Indonesian loves a balanced sentence. These connectors frame the two halves of an argument; learn them as fixed phrases, commas included.

head: Connector
Job
Example
rows: on the one hand … on the other
*Di satu sisi murah, di sisi lain lambat.*

after: ⚠️ It is *di sisi lain*, not *di lain sisi* — the word order of the English "other side" tempts learners, and the result sounds like a translation. The same applies to *di satu pihak … di pihak lain*, a slightly more political variant.
*Namun demikian* and *meskipun demikian* both open a new sentence. Inside one sentence, use a plain *namun* or *tetapi*.

grammars.title: Conceding before you push back
body: Good arguers give something away first. Indonesian has a ladder of concessions, from the essay to the kitchen table.
after: Notice that every concession is followed by a contrast word — *namun, tetapi, tapi, cuma*. A concession with nothing after it is simply agreement, and Dewi will print it as such.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Artikel Mbak Dewi tayang
dialogs.intro: Two days later, a Friday morning. Fajar, Sarah's deputy and a born-and-bred Jakartan, has found Dewi's piece on the paper's website and reads it aloud across the desk.

lines.speaker: Fajar:
lines.text: Mbak, artikel Mbak Dewi udah tayang. Judulnya “Jembatan yang Belum Sampai ke Timur”.
lines.id: Dewi's article is up. It's called “The Bridge That Hasn't Reached the East Yet”.
lines.literal: Miss, article Miss Dewi already aired. title-its bridge that not-yet arrive to east.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Waduh. Nadanya gimana? Galak?
lines.id: Oh dear. What's the tone? Harsh?
lines.literal: oh-dear. tone-its how? fierce?

lines.speaker: Fajar:
lines.text: Nggak juga. Dengerin nih: “Di satu sisi, program ini membuka pintu. Di sisi lain, pintu itu masih lebih dekat ke Jakarta.”
lines.id: Not really. Listen: “On the one hand, the programme opens a door. On the other, that door is still closer to Jakarta.”
lines.literal: not also. listen [nih]: at one side, programme this open door. at side other, door that still more near to Jakarta.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Hmm, itu adil sih. Terus?
lines.id: Hmm, that's fair, actually. And then?
lines.literal: hmm, that fair [sih]. then?

lines.speaker: Fajar:
lines.text: “Oleh sebab itu, janji kuota empat puluh persen patut dikawal.” Artinya bakal ditagih, Mbak.
lines.id: “For that reason, the forty per cent pledge deserves close watching.” Meaning they'll hold us to it.
lines.literal: by reason that, promise quota four ten percent deserve be-escorted. meaning-its will be-billed, Miss.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Bagus, dong. Berarti kita dapat pengawas gratis.
lines.id: Good, then. That means we get a free watchdog.
lines.literal: good [dong]. means we get supervisor free.

lines.speaker: Fajar:
lines.text: Kutipan Mbak juga dimuat, utuh. Nggak dipelintir.
lines.id: Your quote's in there too, in full. Not twisted.
lines.literal: quote Miss also is-loaded, whole. not is-twisted.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Syukurlah. Paragraf terakhirnya gimana?
lines.id: Thank goodness. How does the last paragraph go?
lines.literal: thankfully. paragraph last-the how?

lines.speaker: Fajar:
lines.text: “Dengan demikian, keberhasilan program ini tidak diukur dari jumlah peserta, melainkan dari siapa yang diajak menyeberang.”
lines.id: “Thus the programme's success is measured not by the number of participants, but by who is invited to cross.”
lines.literal: with thus, success programme this not is-measured from number participant, but-rather from who that is-invited cross.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Wah, kalimatnya bagus. Tolong kirim ke Pak Hendra, ya, sebelum beliau baca duluan dari orang lain.
lines.id: Wow, that's a good line. Please send it to Pak Hendra before he reads it somewhere else first.
lines.literal: wow, sentence-its good. please send to Mr Hendra, [ya], before he read first from person other.

notes: **Udah tayang.** Online articles, TV programmes and videos *tayang* — "air, go live". A printed article *terbit* or, in newsroom talk, *naik cetak*. Fajar's *udah, dengerin, nggak, terus, gimana* are everyday Jakarta; the standard equivalents are *sudah, dengarkan, tidak, lalu, bagaimana*.

**Patut dikawal.** *Kawal* means "to escort, to guard" — the police escort a convoy (*mengawal*). In public-affairs writing, *mengawal* a promise, a law or a budget means watching it until it is delivered. Editorials use it constantly: *mengawal kebijakan, mengawal proses pemilu*.

**Bakal ditagih.** *Menagih* is to collect a debt; *menagih janji* is to call in a promise. *Bakal* is the spoken "going to" (standard *akan*). Sarah's cheerful *Bagus, dong* is exactly the right public attitude: welcome scrutiny.

**Dimuat, dipelintir.** A newspaper *memuat* ("loads, carries") an article or a quote; *dimuat* = "was carried, was printed". *Dipelintir* — "twisted", like wringing out a cloth — is what every interviewee fears. Its noun, *pelintiran*, is common in political reporting.

**Tidak … melainkan.** "Not X but rather Y". *Melainkan* only ever follows a negation, and it replaces one idea with another. Editors prefer it to *tetapi* here, because *tetapi* merely contrasts: *Dia tidak kaya, tetapi bahagia* (not rich but happy) vs *Dia tidak kaya, melainkan miskin* (not rich but, in fact, poor).

**Sebelum beliau baca duluan.** *Duluan* is spoken for "first, before someone else". Sarah uses *beliau*, the respectful "he/she", even in a casual sentence about her director — and she is right that a boss should never learn about his own programme from someone else's forwarded link.

grammars.title: The skeleton of an opinion piece
body: Dewi's article follows the classic Indonesian opinion structure. Each move has its favourite markers, and once you know them you can skim an editorial in a minute.

head: Move
Typical markers
In Dewi's article
rows: *Oleh sebab itu…, Oleh karena itu…, Maka…*

after: *Oleh sebab itu* and *oleh karena itu* are interchangeable ("for that reason"); *maka dari itu* is the same idea in a more spoken key. *Dengan demikian* ("thus, in this way") draws the final conclusion and usually appears only once, near the end.

sections.title: Finding your way round a newspaper

blocks.text: Indonesian papers separate news from opinion as British ones do, and each section has a name you will see on the website menu. The unsigned editorial is the paper's own voice; everything signed is one person's view.

head: Indonesian
What it is
English
rows: signed article by a writer or expert
the main story of the day
legal right to respond to a report

blocks.text: *Hak jawab* is not just etiquette: Indonesia's Press Law obliges a paper to publish a reply from someone it has reported on. If Dewi had twisted Sarah's quote, the correct response would have been a *hak jawab*, not an angry post.
When colleagues discuss an article, the connectors of the editorial give way to quick spoken verdicts. These range from generous to sharp; the tone column tells you how each lands.

head: Indonesian
Tone
English
rows: I don't quite agree with the second point.
The data is a bit thin.
It's a bit over the top.
Isn't that a dig at us?

blocks.text: *Nyindir* (standard *menyindir*) is "to make a veiled dig" — a very Indonesian skill, since open criticism is often avoided. A *sindiran* can be so polite that only the target notices it.

blocks.title: Talking to a journalist
items: *Boleh saya tahu ini untuk rubrik apa?* — May I ask which section this is for?
*Yang tadi itu tidak untuk dikutip, ya.* — What I just said is not for quotation.
*Boleh saya lihat kutipannya sebelum dimuat?* — Could I see the quote before it's published?
*Untuk angka pastinya, silakan hubungi bagian humas.* — For exact figures, please contact our press office.

blocks.text: Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.

head: English
Indonesian
rows: Sarah, your opening sentence is good, but there's a ‘di mana’ in the wrong place.
*Sarah, kalimat pembukamu sudah bagus, tapi ada ‘di mana’ yang salah tempat.*
Exactly. The same goes for ‘yang mana’ for ‘which’. Plain ‘yang’ is enough.
Then shall I open the recommendation with ‘Taking the survey results into account, …’?
*Lalu rekomendasinya saya awali dengan ‘Dengan mempertimbangkan hasil survei, …’?*
The data's solid. Three hundred teachers, twelve schools, two countries.
*Datanya kuat, Bu. Tiga ratus guru, dua belas sekolah, dua negara.*
That's it. ‘Saling’ is enough. Next sentence?

vocab.en: to be of the opinion, to argue
to benefit, to be profitable for
to air, to go live (online, TV)
to escort; to keep watch over (a promise, policy)
to collect (a debt); to call in (a promise)

items: It cannot be denied that the budget is limited.
On the one hand the programme is popular; on the other hand it is expensive.

For that reason, the promise must be watched closely.

sisi / di / lain / mahal / biayanya

dikawal / janji / patut / itu
sependapat / kurang / saya

Tidak dapat dimungkiri bahwa itu benar. — Di sisi lain, biayanya mahal. — Boleh saya kutip kalimat itu? — Janji itu patut dikawal. — Saya kurang sependapat. — Dengan demikian, program itu berhasil.
